title: The Lantern Keeper
synopsis: When a silent lighthouse begins sending messages to an empty sea, a young mapmaker discovers that her quiet town has forgotten something important.
bible: Mara is a practical adult mapmaker. Elian is an elderly lighthouse keeper. Setting: the coastal town of Bellweather. Gentle fantasy. Third-person past tense. The lighthouse preserves memories of people lost at sea. No resurrection; remembering allows the town to grieve.
outline: Mara sees a light and finds an old map.
The keeper reveals a forgotten promise.
Mara returns the names to the town and the light rests.

preset.preferences: A gentle mystery in a coastal town.

chapters.title: 1 · A Light Across the Water
chapters.summary: Mara notices the lighthouse and discovers a hidden list of names on an old map.
chapters.memory: Mara saw the light. An old map contains three names: Ada, Tomas, and June. She will visit Elian.
chapters.text:
The lighthouse had been dark for seven years. On Tuesday evening, it began to shine again.

Mara noticed it from the window of her little map shop. The light moved across the water, slowly and carefully, as if someone were searching for a lost key. It passed the fishing boats. It passed the stone wall. Then it stopped on her window.

She put down her pencil.

“That is strange,” she said to the empty room.

Outside, rain was drawing thin lines on the glass. The street smelled of salt and wet wood. Most of the shops had already closed, but a warm light still shone from the bakery across the road.

Mara opened her door. “Did you see that?” she called to the baker.

“See what?” he asked.

“The lighthouse.”

The baker looked towards the hill. The tower stood dark against the evening sky.

“Nothing there,” he said gently. “Perhaps you have been working too long.”

Mara did not argue. She went inside and checked the window. On the table below it lay a map she had bought that morning. It was a map of Bellweather, but some of its streets had different names. The harbour was smaller. The lighthouse was marked with a tiny golden star.

Now, where the light had touched the paper, three names were visible. Ada. Tomas. June.

She ran her finger beside them. The ink was dry, and the paper felt ordinary. Yet she was certain the names had not been there before.

Mara found her coat. At the door, she paused to take the map. There was only one person in town who still had a key to the lighthouse, and she knew where he lived.

The light appeared once more as she stepped into the rain. This time, it seemed almost patient.

chapters.title: 2 · The Keeper’s Promise
chapters.summary: Elian explains the light remembers three people lost at sea, whose names faded from public memory.
chapters.memory: Elian promised to keep Ada, Tomas and June in memory. The lighthouse needs their names restored publicly. Mara will inscribe them on her town map.
chapters.text:
Elian lived at the top of a steep street, in a house with blue steps. When Mara knocked, he opened the door before she could knock again.

“I wondered when you would come,” he said.

She held up the map. “Then you know about these names.”

Elian stepped aside. His kitchen was small and warm. A kettle waited on the stove. On the wall hung a photograph of three people standing beside a fishing boat.

“Ada was my sister,” he said. “Tomas was her husband. June was their friend. They sailed out during the winter storm, twenty years ago. They were trying to help another boat.”

Mara looked at the photograph. Ada was laughing. June had one hand raised against the sun.

“Did they come back?”

“No.” Elian poured the tea carefully. “For a long time, we spoke about them. We put flowers on the harbour wall. Then people moved away. Children grew up. The little sign with their names broke during a storm. I meant to repair it.”

He sat down. “But I did not.”

Mara waited. She had learned, through making maps, that empty spaces often needed time.

“The lighthouse was built to guide people home,” he continued. “But sometimes it keeps something else safe. A name. A promise. A thing we are not ready to lose.”

“Can it bring them back?” she asked.

Elian shook his head. “No light can do that.”

For a moment, there was only the sound of the kettle.

“Then what does it want?”

“Perhaps it wants us to remember together. I have been remembering alone for too long.”

Mara spread the map on the table. The three names seemed clearer here. She thought of the blank space beside the harbour on her new map, the one she was making for the town hall.

“I have an idea,” she said.

Elian looked at her, and for the first time that evening, he smiled.

chapters.title: 3 · A Place for Their Names
chapters.summary: Mara adds the names and story to the town map. The townspeople gather; the lighthouse rests.
chapters.memory: Complete: the names are restored to the town map and a harbour sign. Elian shares his memories. The lighthouse goes dark peacefully.
chapters.text:
On Saturday morning, Mara carried her new map to the town hall. Elian walked beside her. Under his arm, he held the photograph in a clean wooden frame.

The baker came out to watch them. “A new map?” he asked.

“An older story,” Mara replied.

They placed the map on the large table by the window. Mara had drawn the harbour in blue and gold. Beside it, in clear black letters, she had written three names. Below them was a short account of the winter storm and the boat that had sailed out to help.

People stopped to read. An old woman touched Ada’s name.

“She taught me to swim,” she said.

The baker looked at Tomas in the photograph. “My father spoke about him. He used to repair our door. I had forgotten his name.”

Soon, the room was full of small stories. Nobody knew everything. Together, they remembered enough.

Elian sat near the window and listened. Then he began to speak as well. He told them how his sister could never keep a plant alive, although she understood every kind of weather. He told them about June’s terrible singing. He laughed, and then he cried a little, and nobody asked him to stop.

That afternoon, the baker offered to make a new sign for the harbour wall. Mara promised to paint the letters.

As evening came, she walked home past the water. The lighthouse shone once. Its warm circle crossed the boats and rested on the town hall. Then the light grew smaller, until it was no brighter than a candle.

At last, it went out.

Mara stood still. This time, the dark tower did not feel empty.

The following morning, she opened her shop and found a new piece of paper. There were other maps to make. But first, she wrote three names at the top of a page, so she would always know where to begin.
